title: Cross Lighting
description: Cross lighting keys subjects from opposite side directions, so each person or each side of a body gets a key and a far rim. It is common in dialogue coverage, stage, and concert work.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Two moral sources, or just two people who both need a face. Sweat on a drummer, a duet, a fight: edges appear on both sides because each lamp is someone else's key.
Theatrical energy comes from the dual rims, not from smoke alone. It is the wrong tool for a single-source room, a motivated night interior with one lamp, or a true split on one face.
If both keys are equally frontal you have flattened the pair. If only one side is keyed, you are back to side lighting.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Place two keys roughly opposite, each about 70 to 110 degrees off the camera-subject axis, often slightly back so they rim as well as key. Hardness is often hard for concerts, softer for dialogue.
Color may match, or each side can carry a different gel (warm versus cool) as two worlds. Flag them off the lens.
Prompt: Cross lighting on [Subject] from two opposing keys, dual rims, theatrical or concert edges on both sides.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it for stage, sweat, or two people who each need a key from the other's side. Do not use it in a one-lamp apartment unless you want that apartment to feel like a concert.

Kicker is a single far-side accent. Three-point lighting uses key, fill, and back, not two opposing keys.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Whiplash cross-lights the band so rims and sweat read from both sides. Concert films and stage sequences in A Star Is Born use opposing keys as the grammar of performance.
Two sources, two edges.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is one side key or a frontal pair of fills. The tell is one rim only, or two flat cheeks.
Fix it by parking hard or medium keys opposite each other, slightly back, and letting each throw a far edge.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is cross lighting in film?
Lighting from opposite sides so a subject or a pair gets keys (and often rims) from both directions. Common in dialogue, stage, and concerts.
Cross lighting vs side lighting
Side lighting is one 90-degree key. Cross lighting is two opposing keys, so both sides of the body or both people have an edge.
When should I use cross lighting?
Use it for stage, concerts, or two-handed coverage that must key both faces. Skip it for a single motivated lamp.
How do I prompt cross lighting for AI image or video?
Specify two opposing keys and dual rims. Name hardness and any color split. Not a single-side face cut.
